title: Heat, temperature, thermal energy
objectives: Distinguish temperature, internal energy and heat; predict the direction of spontaneous heat transfer; explain why sample size matters.
difficulty: Beginner through application; final question is a challenge
instructions: Show reasoning and units. Use a calculator when useful. For conversions use 273.15 and 4.184 J/cal. Numeric checking alone cannot award reasoning points.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines heat? A. The temperature of an object. B. Energy transferred because of a temperature difference. C. The number of particles. D. Energy permanently stored as a substance.
choices: B. Energy transfer due to temperature difference

questions.prompt: A 42 °C block touches a 17 °C block. State the initial direction of net heat transfer and its cause.
A 40 g water sample and a 400 g water sample are both at 22 °C. Compare their temperatures and their total internal energies under the same phase and conditions.
Rewrite this sentence: “The cup contains heat, measured in degrees Celsius.”
No work occurs. A sample receives 460 J and transfers 125 J out. Find its net internal-energy change. Show the subtraction.
A student says a 90 °C drop must have more total internal energy than a large 40 °C bucket of the same water. Explain why the stated temperatures do not prove the claim.
Draw two objects, each at 25 °C, in thermal contact. Label the net heat transfer and state whether their particles have stopped moving.
Challenge: A metal piece loses 240 J while water gains 205 J. No work occurs. How much energy goes to other surroundings? Explain why this need not violate conservation.
